answers.text: Tell it to always give back the same three lines, same order: date, item and quantity, then any change. Line one is the date alone, line two is item and quantity together, line three is the change or 'none'.
Ask for one line per claim — date, amount, category, submitter — with a total at the bottom.
The dates in this don't quite line up. The email says the 19th is three days from today, but the call it references was the 14th, five days off.
The 62 versus 54 works out to about 15%, so that bit's fine.
Output 2's the one I'd approve, it doesn't just give a number. You can't see the sales or returns totals behind Output 1's number.
Reply 2's the one I'd send as-is, it names the order and the credit.

I'd write a short memo covering the key points of the contract — who the supplier is, the main pricing terms, and when deliveries are due, so anyone reading it quickly understands the deal. I'd keep it to one page and use plain language.
I'd add a step where someone checks the totals against the system before it goes out. That check sits right before the report goes to my manager, not vaguely 'during the week'.
Step 1, where it reads the order and pulls the items, is where a mistake would start.
